The reporting of such cases by palace memorial explains the apparent surge of cases of mad parenticide that took place in the 1760s and 70s. I have found 17 cases from 1766 to 1777 in the Grand Council archives (LFZZ; the date of the report and the identity of the victim are indicated in parentheses): mf 087.1413 (QL31.9.22; father), mf 087.1433 (QL31.10.6; mother), mf 087.1479 (QL32.2.6; father), mf 087.1506 (QL32.6.29; mother), mf 087.1588 (QL33.5.26; mother), mf 087.1614 (QL33.7.6; father), mf 087.1620 (QL33.7.8; mother), mf 087.1655 (QL33.9.28; father), mf 087.1663 (QL33.11.26; “stepmother” 繼母), mf 087.1886 (QL38.9.18; father), mf 097.1112 (QL39.3.16; mother), mf 097.1285 (QL39.5.24; mother), mf 087.2284 (QL41.5.29; mother), mf 087.2341 (QL41.7.26; father’s sister 親姑), mf 087.2465 (QL42.4.18; father), mf 087.2636 (QL42.4.25; mother). The Daoguang emperor (r. 1821-1850) adopted the same approach as Qianlong. In 1823, an imperial edict was turned into a law mandating that the crime of “striking one’s parents to death” should be sentenced to death by dismemberment regardless of whether madness was involved.
